title: Redwood Structured Output & Function Calling Demo - Aurora Analytics
summary: Intro demo of Redwood structured output (JSON mode) and function/tool calling. Covered schemas, strict vs lax validation, guardrails, error handling, and POC next steps including perf benchmark and security materials.
transcript:
Header: 2026-12-22 16:00 PST | Duration 46m
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Luis Ortega (Redwood SE), Sara Patel (Aurora CTO), Mark Reynolds (Lead ML Eng), Priya Singh (Product)

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, can you hear me OK?
[00:03] Sara: yeah loud and clear - thanks Maya. excited to see the structured output stuff we've been reading about
[00:10] Maya: cool, quick agenda - show JSON mode + schemas, function/tool calling with a small demo, go over guardrails and failure modes, then Q&A and next steps
[00:18] Luis: hi all i'm luis i'll do the deep dive demo. heads up audio may drop slightly when i screenshare
[00:22] Mark: noted, we care about latency and also deterministic schemas for downstream ETL
[00:27] Maya: perfect - feel free to interrupt, Sara mentioned compliance and SSO earlier? any hard constraints?
[00:33] Sara: SOC2 is table stakes for us, plus we need SSO (saml) and audit logs. interested in private deploy options or dedicated
[00:40] Luis: ok great, we have hosted + dedicated + private. for SOC2 we can share our compliance pack. private adds VPC + customer KMS and audit logging - there might also be an on-prem path if required
[00:52] Priya: timeline wise we want a POC in january, budget / procurement in feb
[00:56] Maya: good, that'll work. demo starts now

[01:12] Luis: switching to the console - first up: JSON mode. the idea is you supply a schema, e.g. a json schema for the response, and the runtime returns either strict validated JSON or a best-effort with annotations depending on policy
[01:30] Luis: here i'm opening a sample schema for a product-extract: {"product_id": "string","price": "number","in_stock": "boolean"} - note transcription may mangle brackets in this export
[01:45] Mark: are we able to enforce types? we need downstream consumers to not break on type errors
[01:50] Luis: yes, we have a strict mode that rejects responses that don't match; we also have auto-correct suggestions and a 'repair' field that returns corrected JSON and confidence
[02:05] Sara: what about function calling? we need to call internal services securely, no plaintext secrets
[02:12] Luis: function calling uses signed calls with short-lived tokens; you can configure what functions are accessible per role and Redwood logs the call with trace ids. for private/dedicated you'll keep tokens inside your network

[03:00] Luis: demo: pass a prompt to the API with response_schema param and function definitions. i'm sending an example prompt "extract product info from this description" - we'll call a 'create_product' function if schema validates
[03:20] (mild typing sounds)
[03:30] Luis: got a response - returning JSON payload that matches schema. note the console shows a validation pane: green for pass, yellow for repaired, red for reject. this one is green
[03:42] Mark: latency on that call?
[03:45] Luis: for the hosted run here it's about 180ms p95 for this short prompt; p50 is 90ms. with dedicated optimized kernels and batching we can push throughput up but will slightly increase tail latency depending on batch size
[03:58] Maya: common tradeoff is cost vs latency - we surfaced suggestions in Redwood Optimize to pick quantization and batch size per route

[04:15] Priya: curious about guardrails - how do we prevent hallucinated product IDs or fabricated URLs?
[04:22] Luis: two layers: schema enforcement plus grounding - you can pass a knowledge base and require functions to validate ids against your DB. also we support 'no hallucination' heuristics and post-validators that run as sync functions
[04:40] Sara: and for GDPR / data residency, can we keep logs in our region?
[04:45] Maya: yes, for private we localize logs; hosted has region options and log retention controls; audit log export supports S3-compatible endpoints and can be encrypted with customer KMS

[05:10] Mark: what happens if JSON is malformed? do we get partial output or an error code?
[05:16] Luis: depends on mode - strict returns a 422 with validation errors; lax returns best-effort plus a 'repair' and 'validation_errors' fields. you can opt into automatic retries with different temperature/seed to try to correct
[05:30] Mark: can we run this in streaming? we need to stream tokens but also maintain valid JSON
[05:36] Luis: yes streaming + structured output is supported with a final validation step. we buffer until the final chunk and validate, and the SDK exposes interim partials with "is_valid": false until completion

[06:05] (brief cross-talk, someone mutes/unmutes)
[06:20] Luis: showing function calling wiring - define functions in the schema, map to internal webhooks, set allowed roles, and Redwood will only allow those calls from the model runtime. example: create_product -> POST /internal/api/products (verified via network allowlist)
[06:45] Sara: that allowlist - is it IP-based or vpc-peering?
[06:48] Luis: both - hosted uses secure egress with IP ranges and can peer with your VPC on dedicated/private

[07:12] Priya: error handling in POC - we need idempotency and retries on our side
[07:18] Luis: you can return call metadata with a request_id and sequence number; Redwood also supports at-least-once or exactly-once semantics depending on your integration pattern

[08:00] Mark: curious about cost - how much overhead for strict validation and function calling?
[08:07] Maya: validation is minimal CPU, cost mostly per token. function calling is an extra small per-call charge (for audit/tracing) but the big levers are batch size, kv caching, and quantization
[08:20] Mark: can we run benchmarks? we have a 10k prompt set
[08:24] Maya: yes please send it. we'll run a perf test on dedicated and hosted to compare p95 and cost per token

[09:05] Luis: quick note on model variants - we route to smaller quantized models for low-cost routes or to full precision for high-fidelity routes; Redwood Optimize recommends which variant per route
[09:20] Mark: for ETL we need deterministic outputs - suggestions about temperature and seeds?
[09:26] Luis: set temperature 0 and use deterministic sampling; we also recommend 'nucleus' off for strict extractors. plus schema enforcement ensures types

[10:00] Priya: any limitations in function calling payload size or concurrency?
[10:05] Luis: payloads up to 1 MB currently, concurrency is per customer quota - dedicated can be increased via reserved capacity

[11:20] (screenshare ends, back to camera)
[11:30] Sara: thanks - this looks promising. a couple of security clarifications: can we rotate KMS keys monthly and have proof of key usage?
[11:38] Maya: yes, customer-managed KMS with rotation, and audit logs include key ids and usage traces

[12:10] Maya: recap and next steps
[12:13] Maya: 1) we'll send pricing and the security pack, 2) set up a perf POC using your 10k prompts, 3) schedule a technical deep dive with infra/networking and our enterprise solutions lead

[12:28] Mark: who owns the perf run on your side?
[12:31] Maya: luis will own the perf test and work with your team to set up credentials

[12:40] Luis: I'll reach out after the call to request the prompt set and a small sample of expected outputs

[12:48] Priya: timeline for the POC kickoff?
[12:51] Maya: aim for first week of january; we'll prepare a short SOW after pricing

[13:05] (a bit of small talk, winter holidays mentioned)
[13:20] Sara: ok thanks everyone, we'll expect materials by end of week
[13:25] Maya: thanks all - end call

Notes: transcription has minor mis-hear errors, product names sometimes split (K V cache), and some timestamps approximate
